articles.title: Air quality alert for Chicago extended through Monday as wildfire smoke from Canada lingers
articles.description:
The Illinois Environmental Protection Agency has extended the Areawide Air Pollution Action Day through Monday as wildfire smoke from Canada continues to affect air quality throughout Illinois.

An EPA alert said particulate pollution is forecast to reach or exceed the “Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups” category in all or nearly all Illinois Air Quality Index forecast sectors Monday.

“For the rest of today and into tomorrow areas both inside and outside of the Action Day coverage area may experience smoke to a varying degree and duration,” said Kim Biggs, public information officer with Illinois EPA.

Residents should check the NowCast AQI to monitor air quality conditions to identify periods of poor and cleaner air quality throughout the day regardless of the level of the daily forecasted Air Quality Index, Biggs said, adding, “This will also be a helpful tip on Monday anywhere in Illinois as smoke levels are likely to significantly decrease over Illinois progressively from southwest to northeast from around midday through the evening hours."

An air quality alert remains in effect through Monday, the National Weather Service said Sunday.

Meteorologist Gino Izzi said visibility has improved considerably since Thursday, when Chicago experienced its worst air quality, and Friday morning, when smoke was much thicker near the surface.

“Meteorologically, the visibility is what’s most impacted by the smoke,” Izzi said. “The thickness of the smoke near the surface is much less today than it was early last week,” he said.

Izzi said stronger southwest winds are expected to develop Monday afternoon and should push any remaining smoke north and east of the Chicago area.

“If there is smoke, it should likely decrease during the afternoon,” Izzi said about Monday’s outlook.

Conditions later in the week are less certain.

Izzi said smoke could potentially return to Chicago on Tuesday night into Wednesday if there are still wildfires burning to the north and a reservoir of smoke remains, though he emphasized that forecast remains highly uncertain.

“Trying to predict how much fire and how much smoke there’s going to be four or five days out is pretty hard to do,” Izzi said.

Cooler and less humid conditions are expected by the end of the week, according to the weather service.

Despite the lingering smoke, many attractions in the city and nearby suburbs were operating normally Sunday, while some made adjustments and continued to monitor air quality conditions.

The Chicago Park District listed beaches as open Sunday on its website but displayed a banner at the top of the page alerting the public that the Illinois EPA had declared an Air Pollution Action Day for the Chicago metro area and that Air Quality Index levels were in the orange category, which may be unhealthy for sensitive groups.

Six Flags Great America and Hurricane Harbor in north suburban Gurnee were operating as usual Sunday.

The Morton Arboretum in west suburban Lisle remained open but canceled outdoor volunteer activities while continuing to monitor air quality conditions, spokesperson Ellyn Fortino said.

Chicago Architecture Center river cruises were also operating as usual. Spokesman Rob Walton said patrons aboard First Lady boats have access to air-conditioned cabins with filtered air.

At the Chicago Botanic Garden in north suburban Glencoe, classes scheduled onsite Sunday were held indoors, while tours and other outdoor offerings continued as usual, spokesperson Erin Benassi said.

Navy Pier said Sunday afternoon that regular programming would proceed as planned but that it would continue to assess conditions throughout the day.

“Navy Pier is continuing to monitor the air quality to ensure the safety and comfort of our guests and dedicated staff,” the pier said in an emailed statement.

Air quality can affect both visitors and animals at the Lincoln Park Zoo, though the zoo remained open on Sunday.

Depending on air quality conditions, spokesperson Anna Cieslik said care teams evaluate whether any animals might experience respiratory issues or otherwise be affected by the smoke.

Animals with outdoor habitats always have access to indoor spaces, and some have chosen to go inside during the recent smoke, she said.

Care teams also adjust animals’ enrichment and feeding strategies to avoid strenuous activity during air quality alerts.

“No animal is being strictly kept inside right now. That’s a call we only like to make in the most extreme situations because it can have an outweighed negative impact on their welfare,” Cieslik said. “But with the air quality we’ve been having lately, some animals are going inside on their own.”

Smoke also affected events around the Chicago area over the weekend.

When Paul Simon came to the stage Saturday night at Ravinia in Highland Park, the singer told the audience he was changing the order of his set because the air quality was getting worse and he was going to perform older songs first in case people needed to leave.

Ravinia said Sunday afternoon that performances by the Steans Institute and the Chicago Symphony Orchestra would proceed as scheduled, while encouraging guests to monitor air quality reports and determine their own comfort level with attending.

Contributing: Lynn Sweet

articles.title: The Strait of Hormuz crisis is exposing a hidden food risk. New fertilizer tech could help
articles.description: When ships can’t make it through the Strait of Hormuz, the fallout goes beyond the price of oil: Nearly a third of the world’s fertilizer also passes through the corridor, coming from factories in countries like Qatar. Fertilizer prices have surged due to the Iran war—and added one more reason that food prices are going up around the world. Better technology could help. Right now most fertilizer is made using the Haber process, a technique developed more than a century ago that starts with natural gas. It’s a major source of emissions, and also a supply chain risk. Countries that don’t have their own large natural gas supplies are the most exposed. The war in Iran, like the the war in Ukraine, has disrupted supplies of both natural gas and fertilizer. [Photo: courtesy NPHarvest] Harvesting nutrients from wastewater A growing number of startups are developing new ways to make fertilizer that can avoid natural gas and the risks that come with it. One approach: capturing fertilizer ingredients from wastewater. A company called Ostara captures nitrogen and phosphorus from multiple wastewater treatment plants in the U.S. and turns it into fertilizer . In Finland, a startup called NPHarvest uses membranes and chemistry to do the same thing with less energy, avoiding the heat and pressure used in similar processes. For wastewater treatment plants that need to meet strict European disposal laws, the approach is less expensive than other options for water treatment. “We help them save money,” says cofounder and business developer Burak Yirmibesoglu. The fertilizer, he says, is a side benefit. Because of the financial model, the startup will be able to sell its fertilizer—now in pilot testing with its first customers—at a lower cost than conventional fertilizer. [Photo: Jari Härkönen/courtesy NPHarvest] Recovered Potential , a startup that spun out of Stanford, uses electricity to help target and recover ammonia from wastewater. “We can selectively extract the ammonia as opposed to all the other materials in the wastewater,” says cofounder and CEO Kindle Williams. “In other words, we zap wastewater until we pull fertilizer out.” An advantage of the technology, Williams says, is that the reactors have a small footprint, so they can be low cost and quick to deploy. The end result is a liquid ammonia fertilizer that can be added during crop irrigation. After a decade in the lab, the company is preparing to begin a pilot with a large customer. There are limits to using wastewater; Williams estimates that wastewater nutrients could offset 20% to 30% of conventional fertilizer needs. And while the economics make sense in places like Europe, strict wastewater regulations need to be in place for it to be feasible. [Photo: Nitricity] Other approaches Some companies have developed biotech solutions to reduce conventional fertilizer use, including Pivot Bio , which utilizes gene-edited microbes that live in the soil by plant roots to help them better absorb nitrogen. Kula Bio , another startup, grows microbes in a bioreactor that can be sprayed on crops, helping the plants pull nitrogen directly from the air . Windfall Bio developed a process to use microbes to turn methane pollution into fertilizer , though the company reportedly shut down after losing a major grant from the U.S. Department of Energy. Nitricity , another startup, makes an organic fertilizer using renewable energy and farm waste, beginning with almond shells in California. It already competes on cost with other organic alternatives, but the company says it could eventually compete with conventional fertilizer as well. [Photo: Nitricity] Nitricity is also developing a process that makes conventional fertilizer by heating up air to high temperatures to fix nitrogen, and then cooling it down with water. “You can use electricity to drive this,” says cofounder and CEO Nicolas Pinkowski. “That’s actually the same process as lightning in a thunderstorm, where lightning heats up air to very high temperatures and water will capture that nitrogen.” Though it’s still in the R&D stage, Pinkowski says it’s a promising product that the company just needs to scale up. Assuming it comes to market, it could be a game changer for the countries that are most reliant on fertilizer imports. “If you can deliver a product at a competitive price, but it’s made closer, and it’s less volatile of a price, that would be a really big deal,” he says. Pinkowski argues that the industry needs to move away from relying on enormous fertilizer plants built near cheap natural gas and instead produce fertilizer closer to the regions where it will be used, with renewable energy powering the process. Disruptions such as a closure of the Strait of Hormuz, Pinkowski says, expose the risks of the current system and could contribute to food shortages worldwide. “We think it is possible to do so economically,” he says. “And the supply chain benefits are absolutely needed.”

articles.title: Situation Report No. 25 Earthquakes in Venezuela 18 July 2026 Time: 9:00 pm
articles.description: Country: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of) Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs Please refer to the attached file. Situation Report No. 24 Earthquakes in Venezuela 18 July 2026 Time: 9:00 pm Highlights Authorities report 1,350 aftershocks since the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes that struck on 24 June. Official toll: 5,119 people dead and 16,740 injured. The United Nations system and its partner organizations continue scaling up the multisectoral response to the emergency. To address the needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months, an additional appeal of US$299 million was launched Situation overview Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). Authorities report 1,350 aftershocks. Twenty-four days since the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of 5,119 people dead and 16,740 injured since the onset of the emergency. Authorities also indicated that 17,907 people lost their homes. The Government response remains focused on the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. On 10 July, United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher announced a US$299 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan to address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months. The addendum complements the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, increasing the target population from 5.5 million to 6.2 million people and raising total funding requirements from US$632 million to US$931 million.
